questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman was readmitted to the hospital 3 days after having had a spontaneous abortion at 18 weeks gestation. On examination, she had a temperature of 38.1°C, pulse 132 beats/minute, blood pressure 85/60 mmHg, diffuse abdominal tenderness to palpation, and significant abdominal and lower extremity swelling. Blood cultures were obtained, and she was started on antibiotics. Within a few hours, her blood cultures were growing grampositive rods.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Clostridium sordellii Clostridium sordellii infections can develop following childbirth or after gynecologic procedures and can also be seen with contaminated lacerations or in intravenous drug users. Patients may not present with high fevers but may have significant leukemoid reaction and hemoconcentration, as well as edema on examination.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q32

questions.question: A woman has a history of intermittent bloody diarrhea for the last month. She presents with hypotension and new hemorrhagic bullae on her lower extremities. A Gram stain of a sample shows Gram-positive rods with subterminal spores and no other cells visible. [image-based question: Gram stain of Gram-positive rods with subterminal spores, no other cells visible]
questions.question_raw: A woman has a history of intermittent bloody diarrhea for the last month. She comes in with hypotension and new hemorrhagic bullae to her lower extremities. A sample is taken, with the gram stain appearing as follows (photo of Gram Positive rods with subterminal spores, no other cells visible on stain):

parts.text: What are two characteristic features on Gram stain?
What organism is this?
What is one risk factor for this condition?
What is the recommended antimicrobial treatment?
What are two other interventions you might consider?

parts_raw.text: a) What are two characteristics features on Gram stain?
b) What organism is this?
c) What is one risk factor for this condition?
d) What is the recommended antimicrobial treatment?
e) What are two other interventions you might consider?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Gram-positive bacilli (rods). (2) Subterminal (or terminal) spores, with a paucity of accompanying inflammatory cells on the stain.
b) Clostridium septicum.
c) Underlying colorectal (or other GI) adenocarcinoma; other risks include hematologic malignancy/neutropenia, cyclic or congenital neutropenia, diabetes, and prior bowel ischemia. The month of bloody diarrhea points to a colonic portal of entry, classically occult colon cancer.
d) High-dose penicillin G (3-4 million units IV q4h) PLUS clindamycin (600-900 mg IV q8h) for antitoxin/protein-synthesis-inhibitory effect. Carbapenem (meropenem/imipenem) is an alternative beta-lactam.
e) (1) Urgent surgical debridement/exploration of involved tissue (source control is essential in clostridial myonecrosis/spontaneous gas gangrene). (2) Aggressive hemodynamic resuscitation and ICU support; hyperbaric oxygen may be considered as an adjunct, and given the association, workup for underlying colon cancer.
questions.beyond_mandell: Penicillin-clindamycin combination and surgical debridement for spontaneous gas gangrene follow standard IDSA SSTI guidance (Stevens et al., IDSA 2014).

cohort_answer.text: Gram stain: Gram positive bacilli, subterminal spores. Organism: Clostridium septicum (if no trauma; C. perfringens if trauma). Risk factor: spontaneous gas gangrene with diarrhea history suggests GI entry, possible undiagnosed adenocarcinoma of colon; also congenital neutropenia or prior radiation to abdomen. Treatment: Penicillin 3-4 million U IV q4h + Clindamycin 600-900mg IV q8h (alternatives imipenem, meropenem or vancomycin). Other interventions: debridement/surgical intervention, hyperbaric oxygen as adjuvant.

questions.question: Clostridium sordellii infection following childbirth or abortion.
questions.question_raw:
Q35 (2006 AM)
Clostridium sordelii infection post-partum/abortion

parts.text: Give four (or six) clinical and laboratory features.

parts_raw.text: A) 4 (or 6) clinical and lab features

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Recent gynecologic/obstetric event: medical or surgical abortion, delivery, or genital trauma (portal of entry). (2) Absence of fever and often minimal or no local pain, despite fulminant illness. (3) Profound, refractory hypotension/shock progressing rapidly to death. (4) Marked hemoconcentration (elevated hematocrit) from capillary leak and third-spacing/edema. (5) Extreme leukocytosis (leukemoid reaction, WBC often >50 x10^9/L) driven by the sordellii virulence factors. (6) Little or no gas in tissues, with peritoneal/pelvic edema and effusions; Gram stain shows motile, spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli producing lethal toxin (TcsL) and hemorrhagic toxin.

cohort_answer.text: Clinical: women after gyne procedures (abortion, delivery, trauma); minimal to no pain, no fever or rash; n/v/abd pain; progressive refractory hypotension. Lab: GPB anaerobe; motile, spore forming; lethal toxin and hemorrhagic toxin; marked neutrophilia and high Hct

questions.question: Clostridium sordellii infection following childbirth or abortion.

parts.text: Give four (or six) clinical and laboratory features.

parts_raw.text: 4 (or 6) clinical and lab features

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Recent abortion (especially medical abortion), postpartum state, or gynecologic procedure/trauma as portal of entry. (2) Absence of fever and characteristically little to no pain despite fulminant disease. (3) Rapidly progressive, refractory hypotension and shock with high mortality. (4) Marked hemoconcentration/high hematocrit from capillary leak with edema and effusions. (5) Striking leukemoid reaction (very high neutrophil count), attributed to sordellii factors preventing leukocyte margination. (6) Anaerobic, motile, spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli producing lethal toxin (TcsL) and hemorrhagic toxin (antigenically related to C. difficile toxins A and B); typically minimal tissue gas.

cohort_answer.text: C. sordellii found in soil, sewage, human GI tracts, and vaginal flora following abortion. Anaerobic, spore-forming, Gram-positive bacilli. Many strains non-pathogenic, but some produce virulent toxins that can be fatal. Produces lethal toxin (LT) and hemorrhagic toxin (HT), causing widespread edema, necrosis and shock. Both LT and HT have antigenic similarity to C. difficile toxin A and B. C. sordellii neuraminidase (NanS) prevents leukocyte margination, leading to high neutrophilia. Generally susceptible to beta-lactams, clindamycin, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol. Presents clinically with rapid deterioration after abortion, postpartum, or gynecological procedure. Absence of fever is common. Absence of gas in tissues is common (consider C. perfringens or Bacteroides sp. if gas present).

questions.question: A patient with bloody bowel movements develops spontaneous necrotizing cellulitis (myonecrosis). The Gram stain shows gram-positive rods with absence of an inflammatory response.
questions.question_raw: Patient with bloody bowel movements, develops spontaneous necrotizing cellulitis. Gram stain given, shows gram positive rods with absence of inflammatory response.

parts.text: Most likely organism?
What are two characteristic features seen on the illustrated Gram stain?
What is one condition directly associated with the acquisition of this infection?

parts_raw.text: Most likely organism?
What are two characteristic features seen on gram stain illustrated?
What is one condition directly associated with the acquisition of this infection?

questions.model_answer:
a) Clostridium septicum. It causes spontaneous (non-traumatic) gas gangrene/necrotizing soft-tissue infection seeded hematogenously from the gut, and in neutropenic enterocolitis C. septicum bacteremia produces a more fulminant, often lethal course.
b) (1) Large, boxcar/rod-shaped gram-positive (often gram-variable) bacilli; (2) subterminal/terminal oval spores with scant-to-absent surrounding neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate.
c) Underlying gastrointestinal (colonic) malignancy, i.e. colon adenocarcinoma (also neutropenia/hematologic malignancy), which permits mucosal breach and hematogenous spread.
questions.beyond_mandell: Gram-stain morphology (boxcar gram-positive/variable bacilli with sparse spores) and the strong association of spontaneous C. septicum myonecrosis with occult colon adenocarcinoma are established clostridial microbiology beyond this chapter; the chapter text only notes C. septicum bacteremia in neutropenic enterocolitis.

cohort_answer.text: Clostridium septicum (spontaneous; C. perfringens more associated with preceding trauma; C. septicum predominant in neutropenia or GI malignancy via hematogenous spread, more aerotolerant). Gram stain: large gram positive/variable bacilli, often pleomorphic in clusters/chains, spores with terminal spore resembling a drumstick. Associated condition: GI malignancy (colon adenocarcinoma)

questions.question: Name the pathogen in each of the following scenarios.

parts.text: Butcher cutting meat with a cellulitis progressing despite cephalexin (gram-positive bacillus, non-haemolytic, vancomycin resistant).
Bullous haemorrhagic lesions with gram-positive bacilli.
Acute myeloid leukaemia patient with a line and bullous skin lesions with gram-positive bacilli.

parts_raw.text: Butcher cutting meat with a cellulitis progressing with cephalexin (GPB non haemolytic, vanco resistant)
Bullous lesions hemorrhagic with GPB
AML with line and bullous skin lesions with GPB

questions.model_answer: a) Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae — an occupational pathogen of butchers/meat and fish handlers; a gram-positive bacillus that is intrinsically vancomycin resistant (a key clue, as vancomycin is often used empirically for gram-positive bacteraemia) and non-/alpha-haemolytic. Penicillin G is the drug of choice; ampicillin, ceftriaxone, or a fluoroquinolone are alternatives. b) Clostridium perfringens (traumatic wound) or Clostridium septicum (spontaneous, gas-forming) — clostridial myonecrosis producing haemorrhagic bullae. c) Clostridium septicum (spontaneous, strongly associated with underlying haematologic malignancy/neutropenic enterocolitis) or Clostridium perfringens; Bacillus cereus is a rarer cause of bullous line-associated lesions in the immunocompromised.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b and c (Clostridium perfringens/septicum, Bacillus cereus) are not covered in the Erysipelothrix chapter text; answers rest on general Mandell/clinical knowledge of clostridial myonecrosis and C. septicum in haematologic malignancy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (pleomorphic nonsporulating GPB, can be alpha-hemolytic, vanco resistant intrinsically; transmitted handling saltwater fish/poultry/meat; tx penicillin or FQ x7-10 days). B) Clostridium perfringens (if traumatic) or Clostridium septicum (if spontaneous). C) Clostridium perfringens (traumatic) or Clostridium septicum (spontaneous); Bacillus cereus (rare in immunocompromised)

questions.question: What is the most likely organism in each of the following scenarios?
questions.question_raw: What is the most likely bug in the following scenarios?

parts.text: Dog bite -> sepsis
Scalp wound cellulitis from fresh water
Common variable immunodeficiency with bloating and diarrhea
Cancer patient with bullous skin lesions and a Gram stain showing gram-positive bacilli

parts_raw.text: Dog bite -> sepsis
Scalp wound cellulitis from fresh water
CVID with bloating and diarrhea
CA patient with bullous skin lesions and Gram stain showing GPBs

questions.model_answer: a) Capnocytophaga canimorsus — a slender gram-negative rod with tapered ends inhabiting the canine oral cavity; classic cause of post-dog-bite sepsis, especially in asplenic, alcohol-abusing, or otherwise immunocompromised patients, and may progress to DIC and purpura fulminans. b) Aeromonas hydrophila — wound infection/cellulitis after fresh-water exposure (others to consider: Plesiomonas, Edwardsiella; salt water: Vibrio vulnificus, Shewanella; and Erysipelothrix from fish/animal handling). c) Giardia duodenalis (lamblia) — the classic cause of chronic bloating and diarrhea in common variable immunodeficiency. d) Clostridium septicum — atraumatic (spontaneous) myonecrosis with bullous skin lesions and gram-positive bacilli, strongly associated with underlying malignancy (colonic adenocarcinoma, hematologic malignancy/neutropenia).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part (a) is covered in this chapter; (b) Aeromonas, (c) Giardia in CVID, and (d) Clostridium septicum/malignancy are established associations from their respective Mandell chapters, not the Capnocytophaga chapter.

cohort_answer.text: 1) Capnocytophaga canimorsus. 2) Aeromonas. Others: Burkholderia, Edwardsiella, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas. Salt water: Vibrio, Shewanella, Erysipelothrix. 3) Giardia. 4) Clostridium septicum (w/o trauma), due to the malignancy

questions.model_answer: a) Clostridium septicum (spontaneous non-traumatic gas gangrene with hemorrhagic bullae in neutropenic/malignancy hosts, associated with colorectal cancer). b) Aeromonas hydrophila (fresh-water necrotizing soft-tissue infection). c) Giardia duodenalis (lamblia) - classic chronic diarrhea in CVID. d) Capnocytophaga canimorsus - splenectomy is a strong risk factor for this dog-bite pathogen.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the dog-bite organism (Capnocytophaga canimorsus) is from this chapter; Clostridium septicum, Aeromonas hydrophila, and Giardia are established associations from general Mandell/ID knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: Clostridium septicum (in immunocompromised can cause gas gangrene without trauma, differentiating from C. perfringens; translocates from GI to hematogenous spread to skin; associated with colorectal CA). Aeromonas hydrophila (fresh water). Giardia lamblia/duodenalis. Capnocytophaga canimorsus.

parts_raw.text: AML - fever hypotensive bullae on legs and GPB and gram stain

questions.model_answer:
a) Clostridium septicum (neutropenic sepsis with gas-gangrene-like bullae; strong association with GI malignancy and leukemia).
b) Giardia lamblia (Giardia duodenalis) - classic cause of chronic diarrhea/bloating in CVID.
c) Streptococcus pneumoniae - the leading cause of overwhelming postsplenectomy sepsis among encapsulated organisms (also Hib and Neisseria meningitidis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Clostridium septicum (part a) and Giardia in CVID (part b) are not from this chapter; standard ID knowledge (Mandell Clostridium and CVID chapters).

cohort_answer.text: AML case: Clostridium septicum. CVID: Giardia lamblia. Asplenic: Pneumococcal sepsis; Meningococcal sepsis; Salmonella; Capnocytophaga; H. influenzae. Freshwater swimmer: Aeromonas spp.
